summary:
Satellites have mapped active fires for 25 years, but the record is split between NASA's MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), and VIIRS sees about five times more fires. Joined naively, fire seems to explode in 2012. We built Agni (অগ্নি, "fire" in Bangla), a web app that harmonizes both sensors into one record in VIIRS-equivalent units, validated by predicting every overlap year from MODIS alone (held-out R² 0.95 on area totals). For any area in Bangladesh, Northeast India and western Myanmar, land managers and responders get a 25-year burning calendar, the fire season, "this month vs history" anomaly labels, a 3D fire map and downloadable evidence.
It matters because MODIS is ending: without harmonization, its 20 years of history become unusable. In the Chittagong Hill Tracts the raw record says fire is increasing; the harmonized record shows it is decreasing.
details:
1. INTRODUCTION: A FIRE RECORD SPLIT IN TWO

Every dry season, from February to April, the hills of the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Bangladesh) and Northeast India burn, much of it from jhum (shifting cultivation). NASA satellites have recorded these fires since 2000, which should give land managers 25 years of history to plan with.

The problem: that history is split between two sensor families. MODIS (Terra 2000, Aqua 2002) sees fires at about 1 km; VIIRS (since 2012) sees them at 375 m and detects about five times more. Joined naively, fire appears to triple overnight in 2012: a fake "fire explosion" made by a sensor switch. And MODIS is ending, so without harmonization 20 years of history become unusable.

Agni (অগ্নি, "fire" in Bangla) is our answer: a web app that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into one validated record and turns it into a burning calendar, anomaly alerts and downloadable evidence for any area.

2. WHAT AGNI DOES

Pick an area (a preset, a drawn polygon or rectangle, or latitude/longitude and a radius) and a date range. Agni shows:

  • Burning calendar: a year × month heatmap of 25 years (colourblind-safe viridis scale, with a table view).
  • Raw vs harmonized: an animation morphs the raw record, with its 2012 jump, into the harmonized one, with uncertainty bands.
  • Fire season: monthly median and P10–P90 range (2003–2022) against the selected year.
  • This month vs history: count, median, percentile rank, ratio, robust z-score and a label (below normal / normal / above normal / extreme).
  • See it from space: one click opens the same day in NASA Worldview with the matching fire layer.
  • Annual trend: Sen's slope with a Mann–Kendall significance test.
  • 3D fire map: every 0.1° cell as a column, played year by year from 2001.
  • Evidence: CSV of every raw hotspot in the area (with the FIRMS acknowledgement and caveats) and of the monthly harmonized series.
  • Hand-over: links to the FIRMS Fire Map and email alerts for live fires, shareable links, and light / dark / device themes.

3. METHODOLOGY: HOW THE HARMONIZATION WORKS

  1. Download. NASA FIRMS archive for lon 86–97°E, lat 20–28°N: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 (S-NPP, NOAA-20), Nov 2000 – Nov 2026, plus near-real-time files: 6.58 million rows.
  2. Clean. Vegetation fires only (FIRMS type 0); MODIS confidence ≥ 30; VIIRS nominal or high: 5.94 million detections. Static sources such as gas flares are removed.
  3. Grid. Every detection goes to a 0.1° cell and month, per sensor: 7,434 active cells, 2.33 million cell-months.
  4. Choose consistent references. MODIS = Terra + Aqua; VIIRS = S-NPP only, so adding NOAA-20 later cannot create a second jump. Terra-only months (Nov 2000 – Jun 2002) are scaled up with wider uncertainty.
  5. Calibrate MODIS onto VIIRS on the 2012–2025 overlap. Four candidate models: a ratio per activity zone, quantile mapping, log-log regression and a local ratio, which learns the VIIRS/MODIS ratio in each 1° tile and season and pulls data-poor tiles toward the regional value.
  6. Validate by leave-one-year-out cross-validation: each overlap year is predicted from MODIS alone, at four spatial levels. The best model is chosen on 1° tile-month totals, about the size of a real user's area.
  7. Continue the record. NASA stopped Suomi NPP data on 2 November 2026, so NOAA-20 is calibrated onto S-NPP (held-out R² 0.992). Agni's record survives two sensor handovers: MODIS to VIIRS, and S-NPP to NOAA-20.

Output: one record in VIIRS-equivalent units, every month flagged by source (observed, calibrated, Terra-only, NOAA-20), with P10–P90 bands. The web app never recomputes the science; it only adds up pre-computed cell-months inside your area.

4. VALIDATION

Held-out results on 1° tile-month totals (detections):

  • Local ratio (selected): R² 0.952, error (nMAE) 21.0 %, bias −0.2 %. Region-month R² 0.984.
  • Quantile mapping: R² 0.875, nMAE 35.6 %. Ratio per zone: R² 0.869, nMAE 34.6 %. Log-log regression: R² 0.571, nMAE 53.4 %.

The 2012 test. MODIS alone has no sensor switch, so its change from 2009–11 to 2012–14 is the truth to match. Raw records jump ×4.28 region-wide and ×3.05 in the Chittagong Hill Tracts; Agni's harmonized record changes ×0.89 and ×0.88, matching MODIS-only (×0.89 and ×0.89).

What we learned. Our first model, one ratio per activity zone, scored R² 0.98 on regional totals and looked excellent. At the size of a user's area it overestimated the Chittagong Hill Tracts before 2012 by about 30 %. The reason: the VIIRS/MODIS ratio ranges from 2.7 to 26 across 1° tiles; about 3 in the jhum hills, where burns are large enough for MODIS, and 6–8 in farmland, where many small fires are seen only by VIIRS. Validating at the scale people actually use exposed this, and the local ratio fixed it.

5. RESULTS: THE CHITTAGONG HILL TRACTS

For the Chittagong Hill Tracts (31,344 km²), the calendar shows a clear February–April jhum season year after year. The raw record says burning is rising: +374 hotspots per year (2003–2025, p = 0.004). The harmonized record says it is falling: −470 hotspots per year (p = 0.001).

Same satellites, opposite conclusion. A planner reading the raw record would think fire is getting worse; the harmonized record shows the opposite. Harmonization does not just tidy a chart, it changes the decision.

The 3D fire map makes the sensor switch visible to anyone: in raw mode, the whole region "catches fire" between 2011 and 2012; in harmonized mode the step is gone.

6. IMPACT: WHO IT IS FOR

  • Fire responders and early-warning teams: "this month vs history" tells them in one glance whether a fire month is unusual, with a percentile and a label, and links to NASA Worldview and FIRMS alerts for the live picture.
  • Land and forest managers: the calendar shows when the burning season starts, peaks and ends in their own area, for planning patrols, burn permits and awareness campaigns.
  • Scientists and journalists: a 25-year record that can be compared across the 2012 switch, with every raw hotspot downloadable as evidence.

Above all, Agni keeps 20 years of MODIS history usable after MODIS ends.

Built for the field. Agni runs in any phone browser at agni-calendar.vercel.app, with no install and no login, so a responder or forest officer can check an area's burning season and this month's anomaly on site. The phone layout is covered by our automated end-to-end tests.

7. WHAT MAKES AGNI CREATIVE

  • Validated at the scale people use. Most harmonizations are judged on big regional totals; we found that hides a 30 % error locally, and built a local calibration that passes at user-area scale.
  • A built-in proof. The "2012 test" compares the harmonized change with MODIS-only, so anyone can check the method in the app itself.
  • Two handovers, not one. When NASA stopped S-NPP on 2 November 2026, two weeks before the hackathon, the record was already continued with NOAA-20.
  • Making the invisible visible. The raw-to-harmonized animation and the 3D map let non-specialists see the sensor artefact disappear.
  • From satellite to ground truth. Every anomaly links to the same day in NASA Worldview, and every number can be downloaded as CSV.

8. TECH STACK

  • Data pipeline: Python 3.12 (pandas, NumPy, psycopg), tested with pytest.
  • Database: PostgreSQL + PostGIS (Neon), Prisma; 1° tile roll-ups keep area queries fast. Raw detections are stored as 1° gzip CSV tiles on Vercel Blob for the CSV export.
  • Web app: Next.js 16 (TypeScript) on Vercel; MapLibre GL (2D map and 3D fire map), Apache ECharts, terra-draw, Tailwind CSS.
  • Quality: GitHub Actions CI/CD with ESLint, type checks, Vitest, pytest and Playwright end-to-end tests, including automated accessibility checks (axe).
  • Accessibility: colourblind-safe viridis colours (never red-green), a table view for every chart, light and dark themes, and animations that respect reduced-motion settings.
  • Open source: https://github.com/mahfuzhasanreza/agni-calendar

9. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK

  • Fires too small for MODIS cannot be recovered one by one. In rare-fire areas such as the Sundarbans, part of the 2012 step remains (×2.57 instead of ×36), so those areas should be compared within the VIIRS era.
  • Single 0.1° cells are much less certain than area totals; preset areas are approximate boxes, not official boundaries.
  • Next: add NOAA-21, nightly near-real-time updates, a Bangla interface, and new regions (the pipeline is region-agnostic).

10. USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

The idea, the product and the scientific approach are our team's. We used Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, to speed up the build: it drafted the implementation plan from our specification, wrote most of the code (pipeline, calibration, validation, web app, tests, CI/CD) and documentation, and ran checks against the data. We made every decision, reviewed the work and verified every reported number against the pipeline output. The figures on this page were laid out with Claude Code and each one is labelled; the screenshots in them are of our own app. The demo video uses our own footage, photos and voice, and was edited with AI-assisted scripts. The app itself uses no AI at runtime.

11. REFERENCES

  • Giglio, L., Schroeder, W., Justice, C. O. (2016). The collection 6 MODIS active fire detection algorithm and fire products. Remote Sensing of Environment, 178, 31–41. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2016.02.054
  • Schroeder, W., Oliva, P., Giglio, L., Csiszar, I. (2014). The New VIIRS 375 m active fire detection data product. Remote Sensing of Environment, 143, 85–96. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2013.12.008
  • Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. JASA, 63, 1379–1389.
  • Duan, N. (1983). Smearing estimate: a nonparametric retransformation method. JASA, 78, 605–610.
